raw_case_text:
A 37-year-old Shepherd presented to the emergency department (ED) with a 10-day history of abdominal pain, vomiting, dizziness, and gait imbalance. He also reported a history of daily low-grade fever over the past 5 months which was associated with fatigue, arthralgia and 10-kg weight loss.
Physical examination was only remarkable for a low-grade fever of 37.8 C orally with a wide-based unsteady gait and scanned speech. Laboratory investigations showed leukocytosis with a shift to the left (WBC count of 20.8*103/ul with 92% neutrophils), normal renal and liver function tests, and a C-reactive protein of <5 mg/l. Brucella antibody test was positive for IgG but not IgM antibodies with a titer of 1:320 for Brucella abortus and 1:160 for Brucella melitensis. The CSF analysis showed predominantly lymphocytic leukocytosis (RBC count 6, WBC count 250, 80% lymphocytes) with high protein (63 mg/dl) and low glucose (1.8 mmol/l compared to 6.5 mmol/l serum level). The CSF gram stain and culture, acid-fast bacilli stain, mycobacterial tuberculosis (TB) PCR, TB Culture, and cryptococcal antigen tests were negative. Also, the patient had a negative QuantiFERON TB gold plus test as well as negative serological markers for HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and syphilis.
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and spine revealed post-gadolinium meningeal enhancement around the brainstem, bilateral V, VII, and VIII cranial nerves, cervical and lumbar spinal meninges as well as enhancement of the ependymal linings (Fig. 1). Also, there was evidence of ventricular enlargement of the third and fourth ventricles consistent with mild hydrocephalus.
The patient was started on triple antibiotics therapy for a presumptive diagnosis of neurobrucellosis including intravenous Ceftriaxone two grams twice daily for 4 weeks plus oral rifampicin 600 mg once daily and doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 6 months. He developed confusion 1 day after starting antimicrobial therapy, so he was commenced on pulse steroid therapy (500 mg methylprednisolone intravenously for 3 days) followed by a tapering dose of oral prednisolone for 1 month. Two days later, his confusion improved. A repeated brucella antibody test showed a decline in the titer to 1:160 for Brucella abortus and Brucella melitensis.
The patient's gait continued to improve, and he was able to walk without assistance. He remained free from headache, vomiting, or fever for 3 weeks. A repeated MRI of the brain at week three post-treatment showed regression of the meningeal enhancement and ventricular dilatation with minimal residual changes (Fig. 2). The patient completed 4 weeks of parenteral ceftriaxone as inpatient, then he was discharged on rifampicin and doxycycline for a minimum duration of 6 months.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 37-year-old male shepherd presented with a 10-day history of abdominal pain, vomiting, dizziness, and gait imbalance, along with a 5-month history of daily low-grade fever, fatigue, arthralgia, and 10-kg weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 37-year-old shepherd presented with abdominal pain, vomiting, dizziness, and gait imbalance for 10 days, preceded by 5 months of daily low-grade fevers associated with fatigue, arthralgia, and a 10-kg weight loss. Following admission and initiation of antimicrobial therapy, he developed acute confusion on hospital day 1, which responded rapidly to corticosteroid pulse therapy.
subjective.past_medical_history: Occupation as a shepherd (chronic exposure to sheep and livestock). Prior chronic medical conditions, hospitalizations, home medications, and allergies not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Abdominal pain, vomiting, dizziness, gait imbalance, daily fever, fatigue, arthralgia, 10-kg weight loss, and in-hospital acute confusion; denies headache. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Body temperature: 37.8 C orally (low-grade fever). Neurological examination: wide-based unsteady gait and scanned speech. Remainder of physical examination was unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC: 20.8*103/ul (92% neutrophils, shift to the left); CRP: <5 mg/l; renal and liver function tests: normal. Serum glucose: 6.5 mmol/l. QuantiFERON TB Gold Plus: negative. Serological markers for HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and syphilis: negative.
objective.advanced_workup:
Lumbar puncture / CSF analysis: predominantly lymphocytic leukocytosis (WBC 250 /ul, 80% lymphocytes; RBC 6 /ul), protein 63 mg/dl, glucose 1.8 mmol/l (serum glucose 6.5 mmol/l). CSF Gram stain, routine bacterial culture, acid-fast bacilli stain, Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR, TB culture, and cryptococcal antigen: all negative.
MRI of brain and spine: post-gadolinium meningeal enhancement around the brainstem, bilateral cranial nerves V, VII, and VIII, and cervical and lumbar spinal meninges, with enhancement of ependymal linings; third and fourth ventricular enlargement consistent with mild hydrocephalus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Neurobrucellosis (meningoencephalitis with cranial polyneuropathies and mild hydrocephalus) caused by Brucella abortus and Brucella melitensis.
Confirmation: Brucella antibody test positive for IgG with titers of 1:320 for Brucella abortus and 1:160 for Brucella melitensis (later declining to 1:160 for both post-treatment).
Differentials ruled out: Tuberculous meningitis (negative CSF AFB stain, TB PCR, TB culture, and negative QuantiFERON TB Gold Plus), cryptococcal meningitis (negative cryptococcal antigen), bacterial meningitis (negative CSF Gram stain and culture), neurosyphilis, HIV, and viral hepatitis.
Treatment & Outcome: Managed with triple antimicrobial therapy: intravenous Ceftriaxone (2 g twice daily for 4 weeks), oral Rifampicin (600 mg once daily for 6 months), and oral Doxycycline (100 mg twice daily for 6 months). For acute confusion occurring 1 day after starting antimicrobials, pulse IV methylprednisolone (500 mg daily for 3 days) was administered followed by a 1-month oral prednisolone taper, with resolution of confusion within 2 days. Gait improved to unassisted ambulation; headache, vomiting, and fevers resolved. Repeat brain MRI at week 3 showed regression of meningeal enhancement and ventricular dilatation. Discharged after completing 4 weeks of IV ceftriaxone to complete 6 months of oral rifampicin and doxycycline.
